question:
A 5-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic by his parents due to a limp that has developed over
the past two days. The child denies pain, but his parents report that he has been favoring his left leg.
He recently recovered from an upper respiratory infection that resolved on its own about a week ago.
His past medical history is unremarkable, and his immunizations are current. Vital signs include a
temperature of 36.6°C (97.9°F), heart rate of 90/min, blood pressure of 126/75 mm Hg, and respiratory

rate of 29/min. On examination, he appears well but has an antalgic gait on the right side. There is no
redness, warmth, or swelling of the joints, but right hip motion is restricted, and mild pain is noted with
internal rotation of the hip. Laboratory results show a white blood cell count of 12,100, erythrocyte
sedimentation rate (ESR) of 22, and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 1.7. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are
negative. What is the most appropriate next step in management? Answer Choices: (A) Bilateral hip
ultrasound with arthrocentesis (B) Intravenous corticosteroids to reduce inflammation (C) Joint
aspiration of the right hip without imaging guidance (D) Empiric antibiotics and observation without
imaging (E) Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right hip (F) Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory
drugs and observation (G) Referral to orthopedic surgery without further testing (H) Bone scan to
evaluate for osteomyelitis (I) Bilateral hip radiographs (J) Continued regular activity
 A. Continued regular activity
B. Empiric antibiotics and observation without imaging
C. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the right hip
D. Bilateral hip ultrasound with arthrocentesis
E. Bone scan to evaluate for osteomyelitis
F. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and observation
G. Bilateral hip radiographs
H. Referral to orthopedic surgery without further testing
I. Intravenous corticosteroids to reduce inflammation
J. Joint aspiration of the right hip without imaging guidance
